Why stop, and only on a few nights

Figures computed from the same data that feed this page.

A broad front that crosses everything

In autumn, 38 of the 43 radar stations on the map see the passage heading between south and south-west, 31 of them with a steadiness of 0.7 or more. It is not a narrow corridor: it is a river of birds hundreds of kilometres wide sweeping France and Iberia towards the Strait. Every wind farm along it is in its way.

A few nights decide it

At the median station, the heaviest 10% of nights carry 54% of the whole season's passage. Stopping on those nights protects a lot; stopping on the rest, little.

And they tend to be calm nights

Tested on 2021-2026 at the 151 zones in Spain and Portugal, the rule would have stopped 7.5 nights per season and zone, for 3.1% of the night output; stopping on every very high night would cost 12.8%. Measured with the forecast itself, which flattens the peaks, it covers 8.8% of the predicted passage.

The radar confirms the chosen nights

On the nights the rule says stop, the nearest radar measured heavy passage 67% of the time; by chance it would be 24%. That is 2.8 times more.

How it is computed

  1. Wind zones

    The turbines mapped in OpenStreetMap are grouped into cells of 0.5° (about 55 × 42 km in Iberia). A cell with 10 turbines or more is a zone, and its forecast point is the centre of its turbines. Countries: Spain, Portugal, France.

  2. How much passage is expected

    The same model as the per-city forecast: it learns from the radar nights of 2021 to 2026 how each night's weather (wind, temperature, pressure, rain) moves migration, and is applied at the zone's point with the Open-Meteo forecast. The level is not absolute: it is set against the zone's own record at the same time of year (ERA5, Copernicus's reconstruction of past weather, 2021-2026). High is above its 75th percentile (what only one night in four exceeds) and very high above its 90th (one in ten).

  3. What stopping costs

    The wind forecast at 100 m over the night hours goes through a generic power curve: nothing below 3 m/s, rated power from 12 m/s and safety cut-out at 25 m/s. Out comes the share of capacity the zone would produce. Below 25%, stopping is cheap; from 50%, expensive.

  4. The suggestion

    The two halves cross in the fixed table below. It is a way of ranking nights, not a stop order: each farm and its monitoring plan decide.

The decision table

stopping is cheapmoderateexpensive
very highstopstop at peak hourswatch
highwatchwatchwatch
moderaterunrunrun
lowrunrunrun

«Stop at peak hours»: with wind, stopping all night already costs; the hours of heaviest passage are enough, usually the first of the night.

What this page does not say

  • Not at rotor height. The radar sees from about 200 m to 3 km; the blades sweep 30 to 200 m above the ground. On ridges, with farms at 800-1,500 m, the two bands come closer, but there is no height per zone.
  • No species. This is nocturnal migration, mostly passerines. The documented mortality at Spanish wind farms is mostly diurnal raptors and soaring birds, and bats: that is not here.
  • Generic curve, OpenStreetMap inventory. Output comes from a generic power curve, not the real machines; capacity and rotor are tagged on only part of the turbines, and the unmapped ones are missing.
  • The nearest radar is far. Tens of kilometres away, and the renewed AEMET radars do worse than the rest (AUC 0.55-0.66 against 0.74 for Spain as a whole; the AUC, area under the ROC curve, measures whether the model ranks heavy nights ahead of light ones: 0.5 is chance and 1 is perfect).
  • In season only. Outside March-May and August-November there is no threshold and no suggestion.
  • Not an order. It is a suggestion to rank nights; it does not replace each farm's monitoring plan nor any decision by the authorities.

Sources

Turbines: © OpenStreetMap contributors (ODbL). Weather forecast: Open-Meteo (CC BY 4.0). Each zone's record: Copernicus ERA5 reanalysis. Radar: vol2bird profiles from Aloft (CC0), the open European archive of bird profiles (vol2bird is the program that sorts bird echoes from rain and insects), over the AEMET, IPMA and Météo-France radars of the European OPERA network. Coasts and borders: Natural Earth.

The code and each night's data (data/wind/forecast.csv) are in the repository.

Public data, rules in plain sight and every figure linked to its source. Leads, not verdicts.

Open, non-profit project. All the code and derived data live at github.com/Asensio94/sub-nocte (MIT licence); the page is regenerated from those same files, so anyone can reproduce what it says.
